name: Serotonin
role: I carry messages between nerve cells in your brain and gut. I'm involved in mood, sleep, appetite and digestion. Mood is shaped by many things at once, so I'm one part of the picture, not the whole story.
supportedBy: Daylight, regular movement, enough sleep and regular meals are linked to me working well.

name: Dopamine
role: I'm part of your brain's reward and motivation system. I'm also involved in movement, attention and learning.
supportedBy: Exercise, enough sleep and finishing small goals are linked to healthy dopamine signalling.

name: Noradrenaline
role: I drive the fight-or-flight response: I raise your heart rate, alertness and attention when you are stressed or in danger. Some people call me norepinephrine.
supportedBy: Slow breathing, movement and sleep help me settle after I have been switched on.

name: Cortisol
role: I'm the main stress hormone. I help you wake up, manage how your body uses energy and respond to stress. I'm normally high in the morning and low at night.
supportedBy: Short sleep, long-lasting stress and a lot of caffeine are linked to more of me. A regular sleep schedule supports my daily rhythm.

name: GABA
role: I'm your brain's main calming signal. I slow nerve activity down and I'm involved in anxiety, stress and sleep.
supportedBy: Sleep and exercise are linked to healthy GABA signalling. Alcohol acts on me, which is one reason it disturbs sleep and mood afterwards.

name: Melatonin
role: Your brain releases me in response to darkness. I help time your body clock and tell your body that it is night.
supportedBy: Bright light in the morning and dim light in the evening support my rhythm. Screens and bright light late at night can delay me.

name: Adenosine
role: I build up in your brain the longer you are awake and make you feel sleepy. I clear while you sleep. Caffeine works by blocking me.
supportedBy: A full night of sleep clears me. Caffeine late in the day hides sleepiness without removing me.

name: Vitamin D
role: Your skin makes me from sunlight, and I'm also found in some foods. You need me for bones, muscles, nerves and the immune system. Low vitamin D has been associated with low mood, although studies do not show that supplements treat depression.
supportedBy: Time outdoors in daylight, oily fish, eggs and fortified foods. In winter at northern latitudes the sun is too weak for your skin to make much of me.

name: Vitamin B12
role: I keep your blood and nerve cells healthy and help make DNA. Low B12 is linked to tiredness, weakness and low mood.
supportedBy: I'm found in meat, fish, eggs and dairy, and in fortified foods. People who eat no animal products usually need fortified foods or a supplement.

name: Iron
role: Your body uses me to make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood. Low iron is linked to tiredness, weakness and trouble concentrating.
supportedBy: I'm found in meat, beans, lentils, spinach and fortified cereals. Regular meals make it easier to get enough of me.

name: Thyroid hormones
role: We set the pace of your metabolism: how fast your body uses energy. Too little of us is linked to tiredness, feeling cold and low mood; too much is linked to anxiety and a fast heartbeat.
supportedBy: Our levels are checked with a blood test. Lasting tiredness or mood changes are worth mentioning to a GP.
